Adult female Ribbon seals attain a total body length of 160 centimeters [Li = 160 centimeters] according to field surveys conducted in the Bering Sea, a dimension that aligns with the slender, elongated body plan characteristic of this pagophilic species. Available data indicate that neonatal pups weigh approximately 10,500 grams [Wwb = approximately 10,500 grams] at birth, a modest mass that reflects the relatively short period of intrauterine development typical of phocid seals. This initial body mass is followed by a rapid phase of mass increase during the suckling interval, driven by the exceptionally high lipid content of the mother's milk. Juvenile animals must accumulate substantial energy reserves before they can sustain the demanding migratory and foraging behaviors required for survival in the seasonally ice-covered environments they inhabit. The species exhibits a clear sexual dimorphism in ultimate body size, with mature females reaching an asymptotic wet weight of 90,000 grams [Wwi = 90,000 grams] according to measurements from specimens collected during the summer molting period. This value places the Ribbon seal among the medium-sized phocids of the North Pacific, with a body mass considerably less than that of the sympatric bearded seal but greater than that of the ringed seal.

Field observations of nursing behavior indicate that the time from birth to weaning is 25 days after birth [tx = 25 days after birth] under the thermal conditions typical of the species' core body temperature of 37 °C [T = 37 °C], a remarkably abbreviated lactation period that is among the shortest recorded for any phocid seal. During this brief interval, pups gain mass at an extraordinary rate, more than tripling their birth weight. At the moment of nutritional independence, newly weaned individuals exhibit a wet weight of approximately 30,000 grams [Wwx = approximately 30,000 grams], a value that represents the culmination of intense maternal investment. This rapid pre-weaning growth trajectory is an adaptation to the ephemeral nature of the pack-ice platform on which pupping occurs, necessitating that pups achieve a sufficient body size to survive on their own before the ice begins to break up. Following weaning, young seals enter a prolonged juvenile phase during which they must learn to forage independently and develop the physiological capacity to undertake long-distance movements across the continental shelf.

Reproduction in Ribbon seals is characterized by a relatively slow pace of life, with females producing a single pup per year [Ri = single pup per year] during the peak of the breeding season in late March through early April. This modest annual reproductive output, combined with the species' extended developmental schedule, yields a maximum reproductive rate of one offspring per 365 days [Ri = one offspring per 365 days] when evaluated at a core body temperature of 37 °C [T = 37 °C]. The gestation period, encompassing both embryonic diapause and active foetal development, spans approximately 274 days [tg = approximately 274 days] under the same thermal regime, with delayed implantation serving to synchronize parturition with optimal at a temperature of 37 °C [T = 37 °C]ice conditions. This reproductive strategy reflects the constraints imposed by a high-latitude environment where prey availability is highly seasonal and the timing of pupping must coincide with the spring phytoplankton bloom and subsequent pulses of zooplankton and fish. The protracted gestation, despite a short active gestation phase, allows females to mate shortly after giving birth while maintaining the flexibility to time parturition advantageously in subsequent years.

Sexual maturation in this species follows a sexually dimorphic schedule, with females attaining puberty at 1,050 days after birth [tp = 1,050 days after birth] when maintained at the species' core temperature of 37 °C [T = 37 °C], equivalent to approximately 2.9 years of age. Males, by contrast, reach this developmental milestone considerably later, achieving reproductive maturity at 1,324 days after birth [tp = 1,324 days after birth] at the same body temperature, or roughly 3.6 years at a temperature of 37 °C [T = 37 °C]. This delay in male maturation is a common pattern among polygynous or promiscuous pinnipeds and is thought to reflect the additional time required for males to attain the body size and social dominance necessary to compete successfully for access to receptive females. The onset of puberty is marked by the first wave of spermatogenesis in males and the first ovulation in females, events that are tightly coupled to the individual's nutritional condition and accumulated energy reserves. In Ribbon seals, attainment of a threshold body mass appears to be a more reliable predictor of sexual maturity than chronological age alone, with females typically reaching puberty when they have achieved approximately 85 percent of their ultimate adult mass.

The maximum lifespan of Ribbon seals is approximately 31 years [am = approximately 31 years] when physiological processes are evaluated at a core temperature of 37 °C [T = 37 °C], based on analyses of growth layers in tooth cementum from harvested individuals. This longevity is comparable to that of other medium-sized phocids such as the harp seal and reflects a life-history strategy that prioritizes adult survival over high annual fecundity. The species' pelagic distribution and reliance on offshore pack-ice habitats may reduce exposure to terrestrial predators and certain anthropogenic threats, contributing to the relatively high survival rates observed in adult age classes. After adulthood is reached, Ribbon seals typically maintain a stable body mass, although females may exhibit significant mass fluctuations associated with the energetic demands of lactation, during which they can lose up to 30 percent of their pre-partum body weight. The oldest known individual from the Bering Sea population was a 31-year-old female, suggesting that reproductive senescence may occur only very late in life, if at all, in this species.
